documents.title: Statin therapy in systemic lupus erythematosus: a meta-analysis of disease activity and inflammatory biomarkers.
documents.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Dyslipidaemia in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) contributes to pathogenesis and cardiovascular risk. The effect of statin therapy on SLE disease activity remains controversial. This meta-analysis systematically evaluates the impact of statins on SLE activity and inflammatory markers.
METHODS: This study adhered to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. A systematic literature search across multiple databases was conducted up to 13 November 2024. Study selection, data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by two reviewers. Meta-analysis was conducted using R software, evaluating outcomes including SLE Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI), C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin-6 (IL-6) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR).
RESULTS: From 3596 identified records, 12 studies were included. Statins significantly reduced SLEDAI in controlled before-after studies (weighted mean difference (WMD)=-0.70, 95% CI -1.16 to -0.23; p=0.0037), but not in parallel controlled trials (WMD=-0.58, 95% CI -1.74 to 0.59; p=0.330; I² = 81.1%). Subgroup analysis showed a pronounced reduction in patients with a mean age <40 years (WMD=-1.60, 95% CI -1.98 to -1.22; p<0.001). Statins lowered CRP in both controlled before-after studies (standardised mean difference (SMD)=-0.38, 95% CI -0.73 to -0.03; p=0.032) and parallel controlled trials (SMD=-1.45, 95% CI -2.84 to -0.07; p=0.040). After excluding an outlier, the reduction in IL-6 became significant (SMD=-0.32, 95% CI -0.63 to -0.00; p=0.048). ESR was also reduced (SMD=-1.81, 95% CI -3.54 to -0.08; p=0.0406). No significant publication bias was detected.
CONCLUSION: Statin therapy may reduce disease activity and inflammation in SLE, with a consistent benefit observed in patients with a mean age <40 years. Significant heterogeneity underscores the need for future rigorously designed, age-stratified randomised trials to confirm these findings and define the target patient population.
PROSPERO REGISTRATION NUMBER: CRD42025630267.
documents.conclusions:
Statin therapy may reduce disease activity and inflammation in SLE, with a consistent benefit observed in patients with a mean age <40 years. Significant heterogeneity underscores the need for future rigorously designed, age-stratified randomised trials to confirm these findings and define the target patient population.

See: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/ . Abstract Objective Dyslipidaemia in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) contributes to pathogenesis and cardiovascular risk. The effect of statin therapy on SLE disease activity remains controversial. This meta-analysis systematically evaluates the impact of statins on SLE activity and inflammatory markers. Methods This study adhered to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. A systematic literature search across multiple databases was conducted up to 13 November 2024. Study selection, data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by two reviewers. Meta-analysis was conducted using R software, evaluating outcomes including SLE Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI), C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin-6 (IL-6) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Results From 3596 identified records, 12 studies were included. Statins significantly reduced SLEDAI in controlled before-after studies (weighted mean difference (WMD)=−0.70, 95% CI −1.16 to −0.23; p=0.0037), but not in parallel controlled trials (WMD=−0.58, 95% CI −1.74 to 0.59; p=0.330; I² = 81.1%). Subgroup analysis showed a pronounced reduction in patients with a mean age <40 years (WMD=−1.60, 95% CI −1.98 to −1.22; p<0.001). Statins lowered CRP in both controlled before-after studies (standardised mean difference (SMD)=−0.38, 95% CI −0.73 to −0.03; p=0.032) and parallel controlled trials (SMD=−1.45, 95% CI −2.84 to −0.07; p=0.040). After excluding an outlier, the reduction in IL-6 became significant (SMD=−0.32, 95% CI −0.63 to −0.00; p=0.048). ESR was also reduced (SMD=−1.81, 95% CI −3.54 to −0.08; p=0.0406). No significant publication bias was detected. Conclusion Statin therapy may reduce disease activity and inflammation in SLE, with a consistent benefit observed in patients with a mean age <40 years. Significant heterogeneity underscores the need for future rigorously designed, age-stratified randomised trials to confirm these findings and define the target patient population. WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC Patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) often present with dyslipidaemia, and the anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects of statins in SLE remain controversial, leading to uncertainty regarding their therapeutic role. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS This meta-analysis is the first to clarify that statins can reduce SLE disease activity and inflammatory markers and identifies patients with a mean age <40 years as the group benefiting most significantly, providing a key basis for precise treatment. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY The findings support considering statins as adjuvant therapy in young patients with active SLE and call for age-stratified randomised trials to optimise clinical guidelines and personalised strategies. Introduction Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a multisystem autoimmune disease marked by autoantibodies against nuclear antigens, immune complex deposition and chronic inflammation. 1 Epidemiologically, its global annual incidence ranges from 1.5 to 11 per 100 000, with prevalence varying from 13 to 7713.5 per 100 000. SLE patients also experience a mortality rate two to three times higher than the general population. 2 SLE patients frequently exhibit dyslipidaemia, characterised by elevated total cholesterol (TC) and low-density lipoprotein. 3 This lipid dysregulation is significantly associated with increased disease activity (as measured by SLE Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI)) 4 and promotes atherosclerosis, contributing to a heightened risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD)—a major cause of morbidity and mortality in this population. 5 Inflammation is central to this CVD risk, 6 with mediators like C-reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) directly promoting endothelial damage and atherosclerosis. 7 8 The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) further serves as an indirect inflammatory marker linked to both overall disease activity and cardiovascular risk. 9 Therefore, modulating lipid metabolism may present a novel therapeutic strategy to mitigate cardiovascular risk in SLE. Statins, as 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-Coenzyme A reductase (HMGCR) inhibitors, are widely used for lipid regulation and cardiovascular protection. 10 Their impact on SLE disease activity, however, remains controversial. Some studies indicate that statins like fluvastatin can reduce SLE activity, lipid levels and inflammation, 11 with reports of improved clinical symptoms in patients. 12 Conversely, other evidence does not support broad benefits in SLE. Animal studies show statins may lower cholesterol without reducing atherosclerosis 13 or affecting immune markers without improving clinical disease parameters. 14 Human studies on statins’ effects on SLE activity have also yielded inconsistent conclusions, 15 16 leaving their precise therapeutic role and mechanisms incompletely understood. This meta-analysis aims to evaluate the effects of statins on SLEDAI and inflammatory biomarkers (CRP, IL-6, ESR) to explore their potential role in modulating SLE-related risk. Our findings may elucidate the immunometabolic effects of statins in SLE and inform clinical decision-making. If dual lipid-lowering and immunomodulatory benefits are confirmed, statins could be integrated into personalised SLE management. Conversely, if benefits are limited to specific subgroups, their applicability and optimal use may require re-evaluation. Method Search strategy This meta-analysis followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 17 guidelines. 17 We systematically searched seven databases (including SCOPUS, Medline, CNKI, PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase and Web of Science) up to 13 November 2024 for human studies without language restrictions. The search strategy combined key terms and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) for ‘Systemic Lupus Erythematosus’ and ‘Statins’. The full search syntax for each database is available in the online supplemental materials . The study protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42025630267). Study selection Original studies meeting the following criteria were included: (i) enrolment of patients clinically diagnosed with SLE according to the American College of Rheumatology criteria; 18 (ii) a statin treatment duration of at least 2 weeks; (iii) controlled trials (including controlled before-after studies and parallel controlled trials) investigating statins in SLE; (iv) clear reporting of outcome measures, including SLEDAI, CRP concentration, IL-6 level or ESR level; and (v) availability of full text and complete information. Studies were excluded if they were: (i) involved patients without a clear diagnosis of SLE; (ii) did not involve statin intervention; (iii) reported incomplete data that lacked or precluded extraction of outcomes including SLEDAI, CRP, IL-6 or ESR; (iv) were non-comparative study designs, such as reviews, case reports, conference abstracts or meta-analyses; (v) had no accessible full text; and (vi) were not clinical studies (eg, animal or cell studies). Data extraction Data from the eligible studies were extracted separately for controlled before-after studies and parallel controlled trials. The extracted data included: (1) name of the first author; (2) year of publication; (3) site of the study; (4) study design (for parallel controlled trials, this specifically entailed recording whether it was a randomised controlled trial and the nature of the control group, eg, placebo or non-placebo; this item was not applicable to controlled before-after studies); (5) number of participants in the statin and control groups; (6) age, gender and body mass index of the study participants; (7) type and duration of statin therapy; (8) standard pharmacologic regimen for SLE; (9) Disease Activity Score at baseline and follow-up; (10) plasma/serum CRP concentration at baseline and follow-up; (11) effect of IL-6 level at baseline and follow-up; and (12) effect of ESR level at baseline and follow-up. In the process of data extraction, some data that could not be extracted directly were combined and processed for sample size, mean and SD by the method described in the article ‘Advanced methods of data extraction for continuous outcomes in meta-analysis’. 19 Quality assessment Two researchers independently extracted relevant data from the included studies. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion and consultation with a third researcher. The controlled studies we incorporated consisted of: (1) controlled before-after studies (ie, single-group studies measuring the same subjects before and after an intervention) and (2) parallel controlled trials (ie, studies assigning participants to different groups for concurrent comparison, which further include randomised controlled trials employing random allocation and non-randomised controlled trials employing non-random allocation). Corresponding authoritative tools were used to assess the risk of bias according to the study design: the NIH Quality Assessment Tool for Before-After (Pre-Post) Studies With No Control Group ( https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health-topics/study-quality-assessment-tools ) was applied to the controlled before-after studies; the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool was used for randomised controlled trials (RCTs); and the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomised Studies of Interventions tool was uniformly used for non-randomised controlled trials. Statistical analysis Statistical analysis was performed using R software and its meta-analysis packages. For continuous outcomes, the weighted mean difference (WMD) or standardised mean difference (SMD) was used as the effect measure, depending on the consistency of measurement scales across studies. 20 Heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic and Cochran’s Q test (significance level p<0.05). A fixed-effects model was applied when I² < 50%; otherwise, a random-effects model was used. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses were conducted to explore population effects and the influence of individual studies. Publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots, Egger’s test 21 and Begg’s test. 22 A p value >0.05 in these tests indicated no significant bias, with Egger’s test serving as the primary reference in case of discrepant results. Patient and public involvement Patients and the public were not involved in the design, conduct or reporting of this research but are being involved in the dissemination of its findings. Results Process and characteristics of inclusion study The initial search identified 3596 records, of which 39 underwent full-text screening. Ultimately, 12 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the meta-analysis. 1116 23 , 32 All 12 studies included data from a controlled before-after design. However, as the study by Zheng et al 32 evaluated a combination therapy of statins and hydroxychloroquine, it was not possible to isolate the effect of statins alone. To avoid confounding bias from hydroxychloroquine, the controlled before-after data from this study were excluded. Consequently, controlled before-after data from 11 studies were included in the analysis. 1116 23 , 31 Furthermore, 6 of the 12 studies employed a parallel controlled design, 1626 , 28 30 32 all of which were included. Since five of these studies contributed data to both the controlled before-after and parallel controlled analyses 1626 , 28 30 with potential participant overlap, a flexible synthesis strategy was adopted to ensure robustness. For outcomes with a sufficient number of studies, data from the two design types were analysed separately. For outcomes with limited data, the more methodologically rigorous or appropriate dataset was selected for pooled analysis. Regarding the specific outcome measures, seven controlled before-after studies 11 16 24 25 27 28 30 and five parallel controlled trials 16 27 28 30 32 provided data eligible for the meta-analysis of disease activity. For CRP levels, data were available from nine controlled before-after studies 1116 23 24 26 , 29 31 and five parallel controlled trials. 1626 , 28 32 The analysis of IL-6 levels included four controlled before-after studies 11 23 24 28 and one parallel controlled trial. 28 Finally, data for ESR levels were derived from two controlled before-after studies 16 23 and two parallel controlled trials. 16 32 A total of 27 articles were excluded for the following reasons: 8 studies were of low quality, and 19 studies had incomplete or insufficient data. A flowchart summarising the study selection process is presented in figure 1 . Figure 1 Flow chart of the number of studies identified and included into the meta-analysis. The demographic characteristics of the included studies are presented in online supplemental table 1 and 2 , and the baseline biochemical parameters are shown in online supplemental tables 3 and 4 . The quality assessment of the controlled before-after studies is detailed in online supplemental table 5 , the risk of bias assessment for the randomised controlled trials is illustrated in online supplemental figure 1 and the risk of bias assessment for the non-randomised controlled trials is summarised in online supplemental table 6 . Overall, the risk of bias for all included studies was assessed as low to moderate. Effect of statin therapy on SLEDAI in SLE This meta-analysis evaluated the effect of statins on SLEDAI in patients with SLE, performing separate analyses according to study design. Subgroup analyses were also conducted to explore potential sources of high heterogeneity observed in the parallel controlled trials. In the analysis of seven controlled before-after studies, 11 16 24 25 27 28 30 the heterogeneity test indicated no significant heterogeneity (I² = 0.0%). Therefore, a fixed-effect model was applied. The pooled analysis ( figure 2A ) demonstrated that statins significantly reduced the SLE disease activity score (WMD=−0.70, 95% CI −1.16 to −0.23; p=0.0037). Begg’s test (p=0.8806) and Egger’s test (p=0.4943) showed no significant publication bias, and the funnel plot was symmetrically distributed, suggesting stable results ( online supplemental figure 2 ). Figure 2 Effect of statin therapy on SLEDAI in SLE. ( A ) Forest plot of controlled before-after studies. ( B ) Forest plot of parallel controlled trials. ( C ) Subgroup analysis by patient mean age. ( D ) Subgroup analysis by study region. SLEDAI, systemic lupus erythematosus Disease Activity Index; WMD, weighted mean difference. However, among the five parallel controlled trials, 16 27 28 30 32 substantial heterogeneity was observed between the studies (I² = 81.1%), and therefore a random-effects model was applied. The pooled analysis ( figure 2B ) showed that the reduction in disease activity associated with statin therapy did not reach statistical significance (WMD=−0.58, 95% CI −1.74 to 0.59; p=0.330). Tests for publication bias did not show significant asymmetry (Begg’s test, p=0.3272; Egger’s test, p=0.1643; Online supplemental file 1 ). Sensitivity analysis using the leave-one-out method revealed that the I² statistic remained above 50% after removing any single study, indicating limited robustness of the pooled result ( online supplemental figure 3 ). To explore the sources of this high heterogeneity, subgroup analyses were conducted. First, stratification by patient age ( figure 2C ) revealed that in the subgroup with a mean age <40 years, 16 30 32 statin treatment significantly reduced disease activity (WMD=−1.60, 95% CI −1.98 to −1.22; p<0.001), with no residual heterogeneity (I² = 0%). In contrast, in the subgroup with a mean age ≥40 years, 27 28 the treatment effect was non-significant (WMD=0.84, 95% CI −0.85 to 2.53; p=0.328), with moderate heterogeneity remaining (I² = 56%). This indicates that age is a significant contributor to the overall heterogeneity, and the treatment effect appears clearer and more consistent in younger patients. Second, subgroup analysis by study region ( figure 2D ) showed a significant effect in the two Asian studies 16 32 (WMD=−1.62, 95% CI −2.00 to −1.23; p<0.001; I² = 0%). In the two studies from the Americas, 28 30 the effect was not significant (WMD=−0.29, 95% CI −1.63 to 1.05; p=0.065), with moderate heterogeneity (I² = 43.5%). Notably, the mean age of participants in the included Asian studies was consistently <40 years, whereas the studies from the Americas included one trial in which the mean participant age was ≥40 years (44.7 years). Therefore, the observed regional differences in effect may be related to the differing age distributions of the study populations, which aligns with the age subgroup findings (ie, age acts as an effect modifier). However, regional differences could also be influenced by other population characteristics or study design factors. Effect of statins on inflammatory biomarkers in SLE This study evaluated three inflammation-related outcome indicators: CRP, IL-6 and ESR. For CRP, as there were sufficient relevant literature, we conducted separate meta-analyses of the effect sizes for both controlled before-after studies and parallel controlled trials. For IL-6 and ESR, due to the limited number of available studies, we combined the two types of research designs for analysis. If the same study reported both controlled before-after studies and parallel controlled trials data, we selected one set of data based on preset criteria for merging to ensure consistency and reliability of the analysis. Effect of statin therapy on CRP levels in SLE Regarding the impact of statin therapy on CRP levels in patients with SLE, a combined analysis was performed on nine controlled before-after studies. 1116 23 24 26 , 29 31 A random-effects model was applied due to substantial heterogeneity among the studies (I² = 73.6%). The analysis ( figure 3A ) indicated that statins significantly reduced CRP levels (SMD=−0.38, 95% CI −0.73 to −0.03; p=0.032). Neither Begg’s test (p=0.211), Egger’s test (p=0.380), nor the funnel plot suggested significant publication bias. Figure 3 Effect of statin therapy on CRP in SLE. ( A ) Forest plot of controlled before-after studies; ( B ) Forest plot of the pooled results after performing leave-one-out sensitivity analysis (excluding the study by 16 ); ( C ) Forest plot of studies measuring high-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP); ( D ) Forest plot of parallel controlled trials; ( E ) Subgroup analysis by patient mean age; ( F ) Subgroup analysis by study region. CRP, C-reactive protein; SLE, systemic lupus erythematosus; SMD, standardised mean difference; WMD, weighted mean difference. To explore the source of heterogeneity, a leave-one-out sensitivity analysis was conducted ( online supplemental figure 4 ). The results ( figure 3B ) showed that after excluding the study by Fatemi et al , 16 heterogeneity markedly decreased (I² = 49%), but the combined effect size was no longer statistically significant (SMD=−0.17, 95% CI −0.34 to 0.01; p=0.068), suggesting this study influenced the stability of the overall results. Considering that differences in CRP assay methods might be an important source of heterogeneity, a further analysis was performed on three studies that exclusively used high-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) detection. 23 24 28 Heterogeneity was very low (I² = 1.9%), so a fixed-effect model was used. The results ( figure 3C ) showed a significant decrease in hs-CRP levels following statin treatment (WMD=−0.53, 95% C −1.06 to −0.00; p=0.048). No significant publication bias was detected for this analysis using Begg’s test (p=0.602) and Egger’s test (p=0.649). For the impact of statins on CRP levels in parallel controlled trials, five studies were included. 1626 , 28 32 A random-effects model analysis ( figure 3D ) showed that statins significantly reduced CRP levels (SMD=−1.45, 95% CI −2.84 to −0.07; p=0.040), but with extremely high heterogeneity among studies (I² = 96.5%). Begg’s test (p=0.142) and Egger’s test (p=0.139) indicated no significant publication bias. Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis revealed that the high heterogeneity was not driven by any single outlier study, as I² did not substantially decrease on removal of any individual trial ( online supplemental figure 5 ). Further subgroup analyses were conducted based on patient age and study region. Stratification by age ( figure 3E ) showed that in the subgroup with a mean age <40 years, 16 32 statins significantly reduced CRP levels (SMD=−3.09, 95% CI −3.93 to −2.25; p<0.001), with moderate heterogeneity (I² = 60.9%). In the subgroup with a mean age ≥40 years, 26 , 28 the effect was not statistically significant (SMD=−0.23, 95% CI −0.62 to 0.17; p=0.262), with I 2 of 47.9%. Subgroup analysis by study region ( figure 3F ) showed the largest and significant effect size in Asian studies 16 32 (SMD=−3.09, 95% CI −3.93 to −2.25; p<0.001; I² = 60.9%). The effect size was smaller but still significant in European studies 26 27 (SMD=−0.44, 95% CI −0.87 to −0.00; p=0.048), with no heterogeneity (I² = 0%). The single study from the Americas 28 was not pooled separately. Notably, the subgroup with a mean age <40 years was identical to the Asian subgroup. These results indicate that both mean age and study region are potential contributors to the high heterogeneity observed in the overall analysis. Effect of statins on IL-6 in SLE A total of 4 controlled before-after studies 11 23 24 28 and one parallel controlled trial 28 reported IL-6 levels. Due to potential population overlap between the parallel controlled trial and one of the controlled before-after studies, data from the four controlled before-after studies were pooled to ensure analytical independence. Fixed-effect model analysis ( figure 4A ) indicated that the overall effect of statins on IL-6 levels was not statistically significant (SMD=−0.12, 95% CI −0.34 to 0.09; p=0.247), with moderate heterogeneity observed (I² = 47.6%). For publication bias, Begg’s test showed marginal significance (p=0.042), while Egger’s test did not (p=0.073). Given this inconsistency, the more sensitive Egger’s test was prioritised, suggesting no significant bias. The corresponding funnel plot is shown in online supplemental figure 6 . Figure 4 Effect of statins on IL-6 in SLE. ( A ) Forest plot of the main analysis; ( B ) Forest plot after sensitivity analysis excluding the study by Petri et al . 28 IL-6, interleukin-6; SLE, systemic lupus erythematosus; SMD, standardised mean difference. Examination of study characteristics revealed that the trial by Petri et al 28 differed substantially from the other three in several aspects: it used a statin dose of 40 mg/day (vs 20 mg/day in others), enrolled patients from the Americas (vs Europe) and included an older patient population (mean age ≥40 years vs <40 years). This study was therefore hypothesised to be a major source of heterogeneity. After excluding Petri et al , a re-analysis of the remaining three studies ( figure 4B ) showed markedly reduced heterogeneity (I² = 35.4%) and a statistically significant pooled effect (SMD=−0.32, 95% CI −0.63 to −0.00; p=0.048). At this point, neither Begg’s test (p=0.117) nor Egger’s test (p=0.231) indicated publication bias. These findings suggest that differences in statin dosage, study region and patient age are important contributors to the heterogeneity observed in the initial analysis. Effect of statins on ESR in SLE Regarding the impact of statin therapy on ESR levels in patients with SLE, a total of two controlled before-after studies 16 23 and two parallel controlled trials 16 32 were identified. As the study by Fatemi et al 16 reported both types of data, the controlled before-after study data from this trial were selected for inclusion to avoid potential duplication of participants. A random-effects model analysis ( figure 5 ) indicated that statin therapy significantly reduced ESR levels (SMD=−1.81, 95% CI −3.54 to −0.08; p=0.0406). However, considerable heterogeneity was observed among the studies (I² = 92.8%). Due to the limited number of included studies, a reliable subgroup analysis to explore specific sources of this heterogeneity could not be performed. Begg’s test (p=0.602), Egger’s test (p=0.740) and the funnel plot are detailed in online supplemental figure 7 . Figure 5 Effect of statins on ESR in SLE. ESR, erythrocyte sedimentation rate; SLE, systemic lupus erythematosus; SMD, standardised mean difference. Discussion This meta-analysis assessed the impact of statin therapy on disease activity and inflammatory biomarkers in SLE. Overall, statins appear to offer benefits in SLE, though the significance and consistency of these effects vary considerably based on study design, patient characteristics and the specific outcome measured. Controlled before-after studies demonstrated a significant and stable reduction in the SLEDAI score with statin treatment, indicating decreased disease activity. This is supported by mechanistic research, such as studies showing atorvastatin reduces plasma levels of CXCL9 (which correlates with SLEDAI) 33 and TNF system molecules (TNF-α, sTNFR1, sTNFR2), 34 potentially impacting both SLE activity and atherosclerosis. However, in higher-evidence parallel controlled trials, the overall effect on disease activity was not statistically significant, with substantial heterogeneity. Some trials reported no effect on SLEDAI, 35 or even isolated cases of disease exacerbation, 27 highlighting inconsistent evidence and the need to explore heterogeneity sources. Subgroup analysis in parallel controlled trials identified patient mean age as a key effect modifier. In subgroups with mean age <40 years, statins showed a clear, consistent benefit in reducing disease activity with no heterogeneity. In contrast, no significant effect was observed in subgroups aged ≥40 years. This aligns with a study finding a stronger association between an adverse lipid ratio (TC/HDL-C) and poor prognosis in lupus nephritis patients under 40. 36 The observed benefit in younger patients may reflect their typically higher disease activity and more prominent immune-inflammatory drive, 37 where statins’ immunomodulatory effects might be more readily translated into clinical benefit. Analysis by region showed a significant effect in Asian studies but not in American studies. Notably, the included Asian studies exclusively involved participants under 40, reinforcing age as a likely primary driver of this regional disparity, although other confounding factors cannot be excluded. Regarding inflammatory biomarkers, CRP is both associated with irreversible organ damage in SLE 38 and serves as a cardiovascular risk marker linked to disease activity. 39 Recent evidence indicates the potential of statins to modulate CRP. 40 Our meta-analysis confirms they significantly reduce CRP levels in SLE patients, although this pooled result exhibited high heterogeneity (I²: 73.6%–96.5%), indicating the effect is not uniform. Subgroup analyses identified key modifiers. In controlled before-after studies, heterogeneity disappeared and a consistent reduction was observed when the analysis was restricted to studies using hs-CRP assays, highlighting assay sensitivity as a major technical source of variability. In parallel controlled trials, the greatest reduction in CRP occurred in studies with a mean patient age below 40 years—a subgroup entirely overlapping with Asian studies—reinforcing younger average age as a critical effect modifier. While regional differences were also evident, a modest effect persisted in European studies involving older patient populations (mean age ≥40 years), suggesting that in these individuals, the anti-inflammatory response may be influenced by a more complex interplay of genetic, phenotypic or methodological factors. The analysis of IL-6 further underscores the importance of population and methodological heterogeneity. As a pivotal cytokine in SLE pathogenesis, IL-6 correlates with disease activity and contributes to cardiovascular complications and complement dysregulation. 41 , 43 While in vitro and some clinical data suggest statins like atorvastatin may reduce IL-6 (eg, by decreasing T-cell production), 44 45 our initial pooled analysis showed no significant overall effect—a finding consistent with other reports. 46 However, after excluding one outlier study (characterised by older mean patient age, American origin and higher statin dose), heterogeneity markedly decreased and the pooled effect became statistically significant. This sensitivity analysis suggests that the effect of statins on IL-6 is sensitive to dosage and specific population traits. Notably, existing literature is contradictory, with one study indicating fluvastatin may even increase IL-6 in certain contexts. 47 These inconsistencies imply that the ultimate impact of statins on IL-6 is shaped by a complex interplay of disease context, statin type and population differences, explaining the high heterogeneity observed in our meta-analysis. Analysis of ESR presents a complex picture. ESR serves not only as a biomarker for SLE disease activity 48 but is also independently associated with coronary atherosclerosis. 49 Furthermore, our pooled analysis suggests an association between statin use and reduced ESR levels; 50 this finding is constrained by extreme heterogeneity (I² = 92.8%). This likely stems from the limited number of studies, variability in study populations and the non-specific nature of ESR, which is easily confounded by common SLE comorbidities like anaemia and hyperglobulinaemia. Therefore, although statins may lower ESR via anti-inflammatory effects, the current evidence is insufficient for a definitive conclusion. This study has limitations. The number of included RCTs is limited, some with small sample sizes, affecting statistical power. Residual heterogeneity persists beyond the explored subgroups, suggesting unmeasured confounders (eg, specific SLE manifestations, concomitant medications, statin type/duration) may influence outcomes. The number of studies for certain biomarkers (eg, IL-6, ESR) was small, restricting conclusions and exploration of heterogeneity. Finally, the conclusions depend on the quality of the primary studies, some of which carry inherent risks of bias. Conclusion This meta-analysis suggests statins may modestly reduce SLE disease activity and inflammation, particularly in younger patients (mean age <40 years), with consistent effects on SLEDAI and CRP. However, high heterogeneity in controlled trials and subgroup-specific benefits preclude broad recommendations. Future large-scale RCTs are needed to define optimal use within personalised SLE management. documents.title: Artificial Intelligence-based detection of neuropsychiatric lupus: an exploratory meta-analysis of neuroimaging and multimodal biomarker models.
documents.abstract: Neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus (NPSLE) remains challenging to diagnose because of heterogeneous clinical presentations, nonspecific findings, and the absence of definitive biomarkers. Artificial intelligence (AI) methods have been increasingly explored using neuroimaging and other biologically informative data to support identification of neuropsychiatric involvement in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). However, the reported performance and methodological robustness of these approaches have not been systematically characterized. To perform an exploratory meta-analysis describing reported diagnostic performance, heterogeneity, and methodological characteristics of AI-based models using neuroimaging and multimodal biomarkers for detecting neuropsychiatric involvement in SLE. We conducted a PRISMA-compliant systematic review of studies applying machine learning or deep learning models to neuroimaging or biologically informative modalities relevant to central nervous system involvement, including structural or functional MRI, magnetic resonance spectroscopy, spectroscopy-based molecular fingerprints, and CSF or serum biomarkers. PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through August 2025. Given substantial heterogeneity in study design, model objectives, input modalities, and validation strategies, analyses were undertaken within an exploratory framework. Random-effects models were used to summarize reported area under the curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Subgroup and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were performed. Fourteen studies involving more than 800 participants were included. Most studies used neuroimaging, particularly resting-state functional MRI, while others incorporated non-imaging biomarkers. Reported performance metrics were generally high (pooled AUC 0.86; accuracy 0.87), but between-study heterogeneity was substantial. Sensitivity analyses demonstrated that pooled estimates were unstable and influenced by individual studies. No clear performance differences were observed between classical machine learning and deep learning approaches. External validation and formal explainable AI methods were uncommon. This exploratory synthesis indicates that AI-based models applied to neuroimaging and multimodal biomarkers have shown promising reported performance in NPSLE. However, marked heterogeneity, limited robustness, and poor interpretability currently preclude firm conclusions regarding clinical applicability. More standardized, externally validated, and interpretable studies are needed before translation into clinical practice.

Affecting up to 40% of individuals with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), neuropsychiatric involvement spans a wide clinical spectrum, from mild cognitive dysfunction and mood disturbances to seizures, psychosis, and cerebrovascular events [ 3 , 4 ]. The heterogeneous presentation, often lacking clear radiological or serological correlates, challenges timely diagnosis and can delay appropriate treatment. Conventional imaging findings are frequently normal or non-specific, and existing diagnostic frameworks rely heavily on exclusion, leading to missed or ambiguous cases, particularly in early or subclinical stages [ 5 , 6 ]. Over the past decade, neuroimaging has evolved as a valuable tool in evaluating central nervous system involvement in SLE. However, the interpretive limitations of conventional approaches have prompted growing interest in computational methods that can capture more subtle, distributed, or nonlinear patterns of brain alteration [ 7 ]. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques, offers the capacity to extract clinically relevant features from high-dimensional neuroimaging data, thereby enabling automated classification that surpasses the capabilities of visual interpretation. Applications of these models in SLE have included structural MRI, functional connectivity mapping, spectroscopy, and multi-parametric fusion, but most studies to date remain exploratory, methodologically varied, and limited in generalizability [ 8 , 9 ]. Despite encouraging early results, it remains unclear whether AI-based models for NPSLE can achieve the level of diagnostic performance required for real-world implementation. Few studies have used external validation datasets, and many lack clarity regarding model transparency, reproducibility, and clinical applicability. Moreover, no prior synthesis has systematically examined the diagnostic performance, methodological quality, and subgroup variability across this emerging body of literature. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies applying AI models to neuroimaging data for the diagnosis of NPSLE. Our primary aim was to explore and summarize reported diagnostic performance metrics, including accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and the area under the curve (AUC), across the existing literature. We additionally examined whether model type (classical machine learning versus deep learning) was associated with differences in reported performance and critically assessed methodological rigor, interpretability, and validation practices. Through this exploratory synthesis, we aim to contextualize the current evidence base, identify sources of heterogeneity, and highlight key methodological gaps that must be addressed before AI-based neuroimaging approaches for NPSLE can be considered for clinical translation. Methods Protocol registration and reporting guidelines This systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted per the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines [ 10 ]. The review protocol was prospectively registered in the Open Science Framework (OSF) under the DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/B7CE3. Literature search strategy A comprehensive search strategy was developed to identify all relevant studies across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection, from database inception to August 1, 2025, without restrictions on language or publication status. The search combined controlled vocabulary terms (e.g., MeSH) with free-text keywords related to lupus, neuropsychiatric manifestations, machine learning, deep learning, and neuroimaging modalities (e.g., MRI, fMRI, MRS). The full search strategy is provided in Table 1 . Manual forward and backward citation tracking was also performed to capture additional eligible studies. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts to identify studies evaluating artificial intelligence–based approaches for detecting neuropsychiatric involvement in systemic lupus erythematosus. Full texts of potentially relevant articles were subsequently reviewed for eligibility. Any discrepancies during screening or full-text assessment were resolved through discussion, with arbitration by a senior reviewer when necessary. The study selection process is summarized in the PRISMA 2020 flow diagram (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 PRISMA 2020 flow diagram detailing the study selection process. A total of 499 records were identified through database searches, with 37 duplicates removed prior to screening. After title and abstract screening of 462 records, 15 full-text reports were assessed for eligibility. One study was excluded due to insufficient or irrelevant data, resulting in 14 studies included in the final synthesis Studies were considered eligible if they met all of the following criteria: [1] included patients with systemic lupus erythematosus and neuropsychiatric manifestations, cognitive impairment, or central nervous system involvement; [2] applied machine learning or deep learning models for diagnostic classification, prediction, or phenotypic discrimination related to neuropsychiatric lupus; [3] utilized neuroimaging and/or biologically informative modalities relevant to central nervous system involvement, including structural or functional MRI, magnetic resonance spectroscopy, spectroscopy-based molecular fingerprints, or CSF/serum biomarkers; and. [4] reported at least one quantitative model performance metric, such as area under the curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, or specificity. Data extraction Two reviewers independently extracted data using a standardized template designed for AI diagnostic accuracy studies. Extracted variables included: authorship and publication year, patient demographics, imaging modality, diagnostic criteria, model type, model objective, reported performance metrics, and key clinical insights. For studies reporting multiple models, the best-performing model based on primary outcome (typically AUC or accuracy) was selected for synthesis. Conflicts in data extraction were resolved by a third reviewer. Statistical analysis Meta-analysis was performed using Stata version 18.0 (StataCorp LLC). A random-effects model (DerSimonian and Laird method) was used to compute pooled estimates of AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity, each with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Forest plots were generated to visualize individual and pooled effect sizes. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic, and potential sources of variation were explored via subgroup and sensitivity analyses.Publication bias was evaluated both visually and statistically. Funnel plots and Galbraith plots were generated to assess asymmetry, and Egger’s regression test was applied to formally detect small-study effects. The Egger’s test yielded p > 0.2, indicating no significant evidence of publication bias. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses For the purpose of subgroup analysis, models were categorized using a pragmatic, study-level operational definition rather than a strict architectural taxonomy. Classical machine learning (ML) models were defined as classifiers that relied on fixed, shallow decision functions (e.g., support vector machines, logistic regression, ensemble tree methods) without hierarchical representation learning. Deep learning (DL) models were defined as approaches that incorporated multi-layer representation learning or iterative optimization frameworks influencing feature learning or model behavior, including recurrent neural networks and hybrid architectures that integrated reinforcement learning–based feature selection or optimization with downstream classifiers. We acknowledge that some hybrid frameworks (e.g., MARL-assisted feature selection followed by SVM classification) do not constitute deep neural networks in the strict architectural sense. These models were grouped with DL approaches because their learning dynamics extend beyond static feature–classifier pipelines and introduce adaptive, multi-stage learning behavior that is conceptually closer to deep or representation-learning paradigms than to conventional ML.To examine whether diagnostic performance varied by algorithmic category, a subgroup analysis was performed by model type (classical machine learning vs. deep learning) using Python (v3.10). Accuracy values were compared using the Kruskal-Wallis test, and results were visualized with Seaborn and Matplotlib libraries. No statistically significant difference was found between groups ( p = 0.5486), suggesting algorithm class was not a major determinant of performance.Additional exploratory analyses were performed to assess outlier influence and robustness of pooled estimates across different model families and imaging inputs. Sensitivity analysis A leave-one-out sensitivity analysis was performed to assess the influence of individual studies on the pooled diagnostic estimates. For each study we recalculated the pooled estimate after excluding that study and recorded the pooled effect and 95% confidence interval. Study-level standard errors were derived from reported 95% confidence intervals using SE = (upperCI − lowerCI)/(2 × 1.96). Random-effects pooling (DerSimonian–Laird) was implemented with statsmodels in Python (v3.10), and the full script and outputs (CSV) are provided in the Supplementary Material to ensure reproducibility.Formal hierarchical diagnostic accuracy models were not applied because included studies addressed heterogeneous prediction tasks and thresholds, limiting interpretability of joint sensitivity–specificity estimation. Result Study selection The study selection process is summarized in the PRISMA flow diagram (Fig. 1 ). A total of 499 records were identified through systematic searches of selected electronic databases. After removing 37 duplicates, 462 unique records underwent title and abstract screening. Of these, 447 were excluded for not meeting inclusion criteria, such as non-relevance to NPSLE, lack of AI model implementation, or absence of imaging-based diagnostics. Following this, 15 full-text articles were retrieved and assessed for eligibility. One study was excluded at this stage due to insufficient reporting of outcome metrics relevant to diagnostic performance (e.g., no accuracy, AUC, sensitivity/specificity values reported). Consequently, 14 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final synthesis (Fig. 1 ). This selection process reflects a highly selective and rigorous screening strategy, ensuring that only studies with quantifiable and comparable AI-based diagnostic outcomes were synthesized. Study characteristics A total of 14 studies met the inclusion criteria (see PRISMA diagram) [ 11 – 24 ]. These studies collectively involved over 800 participants, including patients diagnosed with neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus (NPSLE) and various control groups (healthy individuals or SLE patients without neuropsychiatric involvement). Sample sizes ranged from 6 to 413 participants, with variable age distributions and disease duration. The majority of included studies adopted the revised 1997 ACR criteria for SLE classification. SLEDAI or comparable disease activity indices were reported in 9 out of 14 studies, providing a reference for the relationships between inflammation and neuroimaging (Supplementary Table 1). Biomarkers and deep learning approaches The most commonly utilized imaging modality was resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) at 1.5 Tesla, employing standard BOLD signal processing pipelines with temporal filtering and denoising strategies (e.g., CompCor). Additional modalities included Proton Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (¹H-MRS) and structural T1/T2/FLAIR MRI sequences. All included studies applied deep learning or machine learning models to derive predictive or diagnostic insights. The dominant model type was a hybrid framework that combined Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) for feature selection with a Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier optimized by a Genetic Algorithm (GA). Other architectures included Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Noise-Immune Extreme Ensemble Learning Machines (NIEELM). Clinical and cognitive correlates Cognitive impairment, psychosis, and memory deficits were the most frequently investigated neuropsychiatric features, reported in 9 out of 14 studies. Several studies linked these symptoms with altered metabolic or functional patterns in key brain regions such as the posterior cingulate cortex, hippocampus, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Notably, multiple studies identified predictive biomarkers spanning 12 to 27 neuroanatomical or spectroscopic regions. These features were selected using feature selection strategies or region-level importance ranking, allowing limited post hoc interpretability at the level of discriminative brain regions or metabolites.However, none of the included studies implemented formal explainable AI (XAI) techniques such as saliency mapping, SHAP, Grad-CAM, or attention-based attribution.For instance, reduced N-acetylaspartate/creatine (NAA/Cr) ratios in the frontal lobe and thalamus were predictive of early NPSLE symptoms in spectroscopy-based studies. Discussion This systematic review and meta-analysis provide the first comprehensive evaluation of AI-based neuroimaging approaches for diagnosing neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus (NPSLE) By synthesizing findings from 14 studies, we synthesize reported diagnostic performance across heterogeneous AI implementations, with a pooled AUC of 0.86, accuracy of 0.87, sensitivity of 0.87, and specificity of 0.82. These results underscore the potential of computational neuroimaging tools to serve as clinically meaningful adjuncts in diagnosing NPSLE, a domain historically challenged by diagnostic ambiguity, nonspecific presentations, and limited biomarker availability. Our subgroup analysis revealed no statistically significant differences in accuracy between deep learning and classical machine learning models, suggesting that algorithmic complexity may be less impactful than data quality, imaging modality, or feature representation. The leave-one-out analysis identified a single study that materially influences the pooled AUC, indicating that our overall estimate is not fully robust to removal of outlying data. This finding is concordant with the high between-study heterogeneity observed in the main meta-analysis and suggests that differences in study design, imaging protocol or validation strategy may underlie the discrepant result. We therefore present pooled results both including and excluding the influential study and emphasize the need for larger, harmonized multi-site datasets and external validation before clinical deployment.Overall, these findings support the growing feasibility of AI-augmented neuroimaging in autoimmune neuropsychiatry. The results of this review extend and contextualize several emerging trends in the literature on lupus neuroimaging and AI applications in medicine. Previous studies in adults with SLE have demonstrated cognitive dysfunction, network disruption, and subclinical MRI abnormalities, but few have explored computational modeling as a diagnostic framework. For example, Simos et al. (2020) reported promising classification accuracy using support vector machines applied to resting-state fMRI in NPSLE, though their analysis lacked external validation.Similarly, Barraclough et al. (2023) used clustering and latent phenotype extraction in adult SLE to uncover neurocognitive subtypes, but without the inclusion of imaging data or supervised classification models. In contrast, our meta-analysis specifically, integrates multiple imaging modalities including fMRI and spectroscopy, and assesses model performance using standard diagnostic metrics such as AUC and sensitivity [ 13 , 14 , 24 ]. Compared to AI applications in other neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders, the diagnostic performance observed here is notably strong. Studies applying machine learning to ADHD, autism, or early-onset psychosis typically report pooled AUCs between 0.75 and 0.84, with greater variability and lower specificity. The relatively higher performance of models in NPSLE may reflect a more distinct neuroinflammatory signal detectable in imaging data, particularly when compared to the more heterogeneous and distributed brain changes seen in developmental disorders [ 25 , 26 ]. These comparisons highlight the untapped potential of neuroimaging biomarkers in autoimmune diseases and reinforce the urgency of dedicated, methodologically rigorous research in this field. Interpretability limitations and the absence of formal explainable AI Despite promising diagnostic metrics, a major limitation across the included studies was the near-complete absence of explainable AI (XAI) frameworks. None of the models reported which features, brain regions, or imaging-derived markers were most influential in driving predictions. In the context of neuropsychiatric disease, where clinicians often rely on pathophysiological plausibility and anatomical correlates, this lack of transparency poses a significant barrier to clinical translation. Given that the thalamus, angular gyrus, precuneus, and fronto-limbic circuits have all been implicated in the neurobiology of NPSLE, model outputs that remain opaque not only reduce trust but also limit the opportunity for mechanistic insight. Without saliency maps, feature attribution scores, or attention mechanisms, it remains unclear whether models are detecting true biological signal or confounded proxies such as scanner differences, noise artifacts, or site-specific variability [ 27 – 29 ]. Furthermore, the failure to incorporate interpretability methods makes it difficult to assess fairness and generalizability across patient subgroups. As AI models move closer to deployment in clinical settings, it is essential that their decisions can be scrutinized, justified, and contextualized by domain experts. The incorporation of modern XAI techniques such as SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations), Grad-CAM, and LIME would substantially improve both the transparency and scientific value of future studies in this field. Explainable AI: toward mechanistic interpretability While the diagnostic performance of AI models in NPSLE is encouraging, clinical adoption hinges on their ability to provide not just accurate classifications, but interpretable reasoning behind those predictions. This is particularly important in neuropsychiatric conditions, where pathophysiology is complex, and decisions often require a mechanistic understanding to guide treatment [ 30 , 31 ]. Explainable AI (XAI) tools are designed to bridge this gap. Techniques such as saliency maps, gradient-based class activation mapping (Grad-CAM), and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) enable researchers to visualize which features in the imaging data most influenced the model’s decision. In neuroimaging, these often translate to highlighted brain regions or voxel clusters that contribute most strongly to a classification.For instance, in the context of NPSLE, these XAI tools could help pinpoint inflammatory or structural abnormalities in regions commonly implicated in neuropsychiatric symptoms, such as the thalamus, hippocampus, anterior cingulate cortex, or basal ganglia. If models consistently assign high attribution scores to the thalamus, for example, this might suggest a mechanistic role for thalamic dysfunction in certain cognitive or mood symptoms associated with SLE. Over time, these patterns could inform hypotheses about disease pathways or even biomarkers for subtyping patients.Despite their potential, none of the studies included in our review incorporated formal XAI pipelines. This represents a missed opportunity, both for increasing clinician trust and for driving forward a biologically grounded understanding of AI outputs. We strongly encourage future researchers to embed these interpretability layers within their model development workflows, not as optional add-ons, but as core components of clinically meaningful design [ 30 ]. Sources and implications of heterogeneity in Neuroimaging-AI Meta-Analyses Substantial between-study heterogeneity is an expected and well-recognized feature of meta-analyses evaluating AI-based neuroimaging models. Unlike traditional diagnostic test accuracy studies that assess a single modality or fixed threshold, neuroimaging-AI pipelines comprise multiple interdependent components, each of which can introduce variability in model performance. First, imaging modality and acquisition parameters differ widely across studies. Included models were trained on resting-state fMRI, structural MRI, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy, often acquired at different field strengths, preprocessing pipelines, and spatial or temporal resolutions. These differences directly affect signal-to-noise characteristics, feature distributions, and downstream model behavior, making performance metrics only partially comparable across studies. Second, feature engineering and representation strategies vary substantially. Some studies relied on handcrafted functional connectivity metrics or regional metabolite ratios, whereas others used high-dimensional voxel-wise features, latent embeddings, or reinforcement learning–based feature selection. Such choices influence model complexity, susceptibility to overfitting, and sensitivity to noise, thereby contributing to heterogeneity even when similar algorithms are used.Third, sample size and validation strategy represent major sources of variability. Many studies included small cohorts and relied on internal cross-validation without independent external testing. Models trained and evaluated on limited or homogeneous datasets are prone to optimistic performance estimates, which can inflate between-study variance when pooled with more conservatively validated models. Differences in data splitting, cross-validation folds, and hyperparameter optimization further compound this effect. Fourth, case definitions and clinical labeling of NPSLE are not uniform across studies. Although most investigations referenced ACR criteria, the operationalization of neuropsychiatric involvement, inclusion of subclinical cases, and choice of control groups (healthy controls versus SLE without neuropsychiatric manifestations) varied considerably. Given the biological and clinical heterogeneity of NPSLE itself, these differences introduce genuine variability rather than purely methodological noise.In this context, the use of a random-effects model is necessary to account for between-study variability by allowing true effect sizes to differ across studies. However, random-effects pooling does not eliminate heterogeneity, nor does it resolve underlying differences in study design, data quality, or modeling assumptions. Pooled estimates should therefore be interpreted as reflecting an average performance across heterogeneous implementations rather than a universally generalizable diagnostic accuracy.Accordingly, the observed heterogeneity underscores the need for standardized imaging protocols, transparent reporting of AI pipelines, external validation, and harmonized case definitions in future studies. Without such alignment, statistical aggregation alone cannot substitute for methodological consistency or biological interpretability in the translation of AI-based neuroimaging tools to clinical practice. Toward causally informed and mechanistic AI models in NPSLE While the diagnostic performance of AI-based neuroimaging models in NPSLE appears promising, most existing approaches remain fundamentally correlational. Models trained solely on statistical associations may be vulnerable to dataset shift, confounding, and limited biological interpretability, particularly when applied across heterogeneous imaging protocols or patient populations. Recent work in medical artificial intelligence has highlighted that the absence of causal structure limits model robustness and clinical trust, even when conventional performance metrics such as AUC or accuracy are high.In complex autoimmune disorders such as NPSLE, neuroimaging abnormalities arise from interacting immunological, vascular, and neuronal processes rather than isolated biomarkers [ 32 , 33 ]. Treating imaging features as independent predictors may therefore obscure underlying disease mechanisms. Emerging causal inference frameworks, including causal discovery algorithms and structural causal models, offer a principled approach to disentangle directional dependencies among immune activity, neural injury, and clinical manifestations. By explicitly modeling these relationships, causally informed AI systems may improve both generalizability and translational relevance [ 34 – 36 ]. Pathway-oriented analyses further reinforce this need by emphasizing mechanistic cascades, such as immune dysregulation leading to neuronal damage, network disruption, and cognitive or psychiatric symptoms. Integrating such biological priors into AI pipelines could allow models not only to classify NPSLE, but also to generate testable hypotheses regarding disease mechanisms and progression. At present, however, the limited reporting and inconsistent implementation of causal or mechanistic modeling in the available literature preclude quantitative synthesis within a meta-analytic framework. Clinical and translational implications The findings of this meta-analysis suggest several important implications for clinical care and the future of rheumatology. These implications should be viewed as forward-looking hypotheses rather than evidence for immediate clinical adoption. First, AI-enhanced neuroimaging may offer a viable route to earlier and more objective diagnosis of NPSLE in patients, particularly in cases where psychiatric symptoms or cognitive decline are misattributed to stress, medications, or psychosocial factors. The ability to detect subtle, non-visible brain abnormalities that precede overt structural damage could transform clinical workflows and allow for more timely therapeutic interventions. Second, reliance on invasive diagnostics such as lumbar puncture, or empirical treatment trials with corticosteroids, could potentially be reduced if validated imaging biomarkers were available to stratify risk and support clinical judgment. From a systems-level perspective, the integration of AI tools into imaging platforms or electronic health records could facilitate real-time decision support, particularly in resource-limited settings where neuroimaging expertise is scarce. Furthermore, while the current body of literature is cross-sectional, the models developed could serve as a foundation for longitudinal monitoring of disease activity, treatment response, or risk of relapse. Finally, these tools could support the shift toward biologically grounded subtyping and personalized medicine in lupus, especially if integrated with serologic, cognitive, and genomic data streams. Such multimodal risk models could enable a more nuanced and mechanistic understanding of neuropsychiatric involvement in systemic autoimmunity. Limitations Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the sample sizes across studies were modest and in many cases underpowered, increasing the likelihood of overfitting and model instability. Most studies did not perform or report external validation using independent test sets, raising concerns about inflated performance metrics and limited generalizability. Second, there was considerable heterogeneity in imaging modalities, preprocessing pipelines, and outcome definitions, complicating direct comparison between studies. The lack of standardized neuroimaging protocols and variable reporting of key parameters such as field strength, feature selection, and data augmentation strategies further limits the reproducibility of findings. Third, demographic and clinical metadata were often underreported. Important covariates such as ethnicity, socioeconomic status, corticosteroid exposure, and disease duration were missing from many studies, precluding subgroup analysis and limiting the ability to assess model bias. This is particularly problematic given the known disparities in lupus epidemiology and outcomes across racial and ethnic groups. Fourth, none of the studies employed longitudinal or prognostic modeling to assess changes in brain structure or function over time. As a result, the clinical utility of these models remains confined to diagnostic classification, rather than disease monitoring or outcome prediction. Fifth, and perhaps most crucially, all included models lacked explainability, which undermines their clinical interpretability and trustworthiness. Without knowing what features are driving predictions, clinicians cannot use these tools to support differential diagnosis, track treatment effects, or counsel families. Lastly, the absence of multi-modal integration, combining imaging data with serologic, cognitive, or behavioral measures, limits the ecological validity of the current models and hinders their alignment with real-world diagnostic complexity. Limitations of algorithmic categorization The subgroup comparison between ML and DL models should be interpreted with caution. The operational categorization necessarily grouped heterogeneous architectures, including hybrid reinforcement-learning-assisted classifiers, under a broad DL label. This pragmatic grouping may dilute true architectural differences between shallow classifiers and fully end-to-end deep neural networks. As a result, the absence of a statistically significant performance difference should not be interpreted as definitive evidence that architectural depth is irrelevant, but rather that, within the current and methodologically heterogeneous literature, model performance appears more strongly influenced by data characteristics, feature engineering, and validation strategy than by nominal algorithm class alone. Influence of individual studies and robustness of the pooled estimate The leave-one-out sensitivity analysis highlights that the pooled diagnostic performance is sensitive to the inclusion of a small number of influential studies. In particular, the study by Simos et al. exerted a notable impact on the pooled AUC, such that its exclusion increased the summary estimate, while exclusion of other studies shifted the pooled AUC downward. This pattern does not indicate an analytical error, but rather reflects the interaction between heterogeneous effect sizes, variable study weights, and limited sample sizes typical of early-stage neuroimaging-AI research.Importantly, the primary pooled AUC of 0.86 should therefore be interpreted as an average effect across heterogeneous implementations, rather than a robust, study-invariant estimate. The observed sensitivity underscores the need for larger, externally validated cohorts and harmonized methodologies to stabilize future meta-analytic estimates. Future directions Looking ahead, a critical next step for the field is the design of longitudinal studies that follow patients with NPSLE over time. Most of the current research is cross-sectional, offering only a static snapshot of brain changes. What we need are cohort studies that track how neuroimaging features evolve with disease activity, treatment, and recovery. Repeated imaging at consistent intervals, such as baseline, six months, and one year, would allow researchers to capture the trajectory of brain involvement, potentially identifying early changes that precede clinical relapse or improvement. Equally important is the integration of imaging data with clinical outcomes. Future models should not only distinguish NPSLE from controls but also correlate with meaningful endpoints like flare frequency, neurocognitive performance, psychiatric symptom scales, and treatment response. These links could help identify imaging-based prognostic markers, guiding decisions about therapy escalation or monitoring intensity [ 37 – 39 ]. Another priority is improving the generalizability and reproducibility of findings. Studies often differ in MRI protocols, image preprocessing, and AI architectures, making it hard to compare results or replicate promising approaches. Multi-site collaborations that use standardized imaging pipelines, harmonized clinical assessments, and shared code repositories could address this limitation and produce models with broader clinical utility. Moreover, AI models need to move beyond performance metrics alone. Interpretability tools, like saliency maps, attention layers, or SHAP plots, should be built into future pipelines to help clinicians understand why a given scan was classified as NPSLE. This kind of transparency is essential if we want these tools to be accepted in real-world practice, especially in a field as nuanced and high-stakes as neuroimmunology. Future research should prioritize the development of causally informed, multimodal AI frameworks for NPSLE. Such approaches should integrate neuroimaging data with immunological markers, clinical variables, and longitudinal outcomes within explicit causal or structural modeling frameworks. Moving beyond correlation-based classifiers toward pathway-aware architectures may enhance robustness to dataset shift, improve interpretability, and align AI outputs more closely with known disease biology. Prospective, multi-center studies with standardized imaging protocols and harmonized clinical phenotyping will be essential to support this transition. Embedding explainable and causal inference methods within these pipelines may ultimately enable AI systems that serve not only as diagnostic aids, but also as tools for mechanistic insight and precision medicine in autoimmune neuropsychiatry. Finally, ongoing work should align with evolving standards like TRIPOD-ML, CLAIM, and SPIRIT-AI, ensuring that studies are methodologically sound, ethically robust, and practically reproducible. Shared datasets and open-access pretrained models will also be key to accelerating progress. In short, the future of AI in NPSLE imaging lies not just in improving accuracy, but in making these tools clinically meaningful, explainable, and ready to support real-world decision-making. documents.title: Risk factors for adverse pregnancy outcomes in systemic lupus erythematosus: a meta-analysis and systemic review.
documents.abstract:
PURPOSE: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a prominent autoimmune disease highly linked to adverse pregnancy outcomes (APOs). Previous research on the risk factors for APOs in SLE pregnancies has been limited by regional constraints or inadequate sample sizes. Comprehensive systematic reviews on this topic remain scarce. To address these research gaps, we conducted a rigorous meta-analysis and systematic review to elucidate the risk factors for APOs in SLE pregnancies.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library systematically searched for articles on risk factors for APOs in SLE pregnancy from initiation to March 25, 2025. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) were calculated using fixed-effect or random-effects models based on heterogeneity (I2). Egger's test was used to assess publication bias.
RESULTS: A total of 43 studies were reviewed. Patients with hypertension, lupus nephritis (LN), high disease activity, low complements, and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS)/positive antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL) were identified as having a higher risk for adverse pregnancy outcomes (APOs). Risk factors for preterm birth included LN, hypertension, disease flares, high disease activity, and APS/aPL. Risk factors for pregnancy loss included APS/aPL, low complements, disease flares, LN, hypertension, thrombocytopenia, and high disease activity. LN was also associated with an increased risk of intrauterine growth restriction and low birth weight.
CONCLUSIONS: This study identified risk factors for APOs in SLE pregnancies. These findings may support early identification of high-risk patients and guide timely interventions to improve maternal and fetal outcomes.
